subtype: Approach: check with a doctor when starting with a health condition [Action]
passage:
I'm Shalini, and I share a flat with Zainab. Last month she announced she wanted to start running, and I expected her to just buy shoes. Instead she went quiet and said, "My dad had heart trouble young. I want to check before I push myself."

She booked a doctor's appointment that same week and wrote down her father's history on a slip of paper. When she came back, she told me the doctor listened, asked questions and named the kinds of activity that suited her to begin with, plus when to return. She stuck the list on the fridge.

I can't tell whether she was nervous or just being careful. She laughed about it, but she didn't start running until after that visit.

qa.q: What did Zainab write on a slip of paper?
qa.a: Her father's history.

qa.q: What might Zainab have been feeling when she said she wanted to check before pushing herself?
qa.a: Zainab may have felt a little worried and wanted to be careful, though Shalini admits it is hard to tell if it was nerves.

qa.q: What could Zainab do if she felt unwell during her first weeks of activity, and why?
qa.a: Zainab could stop and contact the doctor, because advice from a professional matters more than pushing on or trusting an app.

qa.q: How does Shalini see Zainab's decision to see a doctor first?
qa.a: Shalini expected Zainab to just buy shoes, so Shalini was surprised, and sees the visit as sensible and considerate of her own body.

grounding: Because of a family history of heart problems, the person asks a doctor which activities suit before increasing effort.

subtype: Approach: reward and track streaks visibly [Action]
passage:
Day 1. Manoj pinned a large calendar to the wall above his desk and hung a red marker on a string. After his first walk-and-jog, he drew a cross on the date. It felt silly and satisfying at once.

Day 8. Harish, his flatmate, pointed at the gap on Sunday. "You missed one." "That's not a miss, that's a rest day," said Manoj, and drew a small green circle. He'd planned it, and his legs were grateful.

Day 21. Fifteen crosses in a row. Manoj noticed he had begun to feel anxious about breaking the chain, and once nearly went out with a sore throat. He wrote on the calendar, in small letters: Streak helps me. It does not own me.

qa.q: What colour marker hung on a string by the calendar?
qa.a: A red marker.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling on Day 21 when he wrote the note in small letters?
qa.a: Manoj felt some anxiety about breaking the chain but also a wish to keep the habit healthy, so he reminded himself the streak was a helper.

qa.q: What could Manoj do if the streak begins to cause stress again, and why?
qa.a: Manoj could count rest days as part of the streak and allow a break when unwell, because a habit is only useful if it does not cause harm.

qa.q: How does Harish see the calendar and the Sunday gap?
qa.a: Harish sees a flatmate proud of the streak; pointing at the gap may be teasing, but the answer shows the rest was planned.

grounding: The person marks a wall calendar after each session and treats a rest day as planned recovery, while an obsessed streak can backfire.

subtype: Approach: push through pain to keep the streak [Pitfall]
passage:
Neelam had run every morning for forty-one days, and her phone app showed the unbroken line of dots. On day forty-two her right knee began to ache on the stairs. She told herself it was just stiffness.

Her friend Vishal, running beside her, said, "You're limping. Stop for today." She shook her head. "I'm not losing the streak." She ran the full loop, her jaw set.

By the weekend she could not bend the knee without wincing. The doctor told her to rest completely. Neelam missed the weeks she had been so afraid to miss, and stared at the app's blank squares, thinking how the streak she protected had cost her the running itself.

qa.q: On which day did Neelam's knee begin to ache?
qa.a: On day forty-two.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she shook her head at Vishal?
qa.a: Neelam was determined and afraid of losing the streak, so pride and fear pushed her to ignore the pain.

qa.q: What could Neelam do when she can run again, and why?
qa.a: Neelam could allow rest days and stop at the first sign of pain, because the aim is running for the long term and not a perfect chain of dots.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt watching Neelam run on?
qa.a: Vishal was probably worried and frustrated, having said clearly that she was limping, and felt helpless as she carried on.

grounding: Determined not to lose a streak, the person ignores knee pain and keeps running, and the injury stops training for weeks.

subtype: Approach: explore fields through conversations with people in them [Action]
passage:
At the community centre canteen, Bidisha, an engineer who kept wondering about data work, opened a notebook and a list of questions. She had promised herself to talk to four people who did the job daily, not to read glossy adverts.

Anand, an analyst, described his typical Tuesday: cleaning messy spreadsheets, meetings about what a chart should say, and very little glamour. The second, a woman from the bank, explained how she had moved in through a short certificate. A third spoke about the range of pay at the start. The fourth said, "Ask to see a real dataset."

Bidisha filled six pages. By the time she left, the job she had imagined was replaced by a more honest one, and she liked it more than before.

qa.q: How many people did Bidisha speak to?
qa.a: Four people.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling as she left the canteen?
qa.a: Bidisha felt encouraged and a little relieved, since the honest picture of the work made her like it more than the glossy one.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do next after these four conversations, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha could try a small task on a real dataset, because doing some of the work shows whether the daily reality suits her.

qa.q: How might Anand see Bidisha's questions about his Tuesday?
qa.a: Anand may enjoy describing the plain truth of the job, since Bidisha seems to want honesty instead of an impressive story.

grounding: An engineer curious about data analysis speaks to four people in the field about daily tasks, pay and entry paths.

subtype: Approach: work backward from the target role's required skills [Thinking]
passage:
Friday night.

Finally did the thing I kept postponing. I saved ten job listings for the role I want, data analyst, and put them side by side in a spreadsheet. Then I listed every skill they asked for. SQL: nine of ten. A spreadsheet tool: ten of ten. A charting tool: seven. Basic statistics: eight. Storytelling with data: five, though in different words.

Then I marked what I already have. Spreadsheets: yes. Statistics: half. SQL: no. Charting: no. So the gap is clear, and it's smaller than I feared. Anjali says to start with SQL because it's what most listings want. I signed up for a course that begins Monday and put one hour every evening in my diary.

The target has picked my study plan.

Salma

qa.q: How many listings asked for SQL?
qa.a: Nine of ten.

qa.q: How does Salma feel about the size of the gap after comparing skills?
qa.a: Salma feels relieved and motivated, since the gap turns out smaller than feared and now has a clear order.

qa.q: What could Salma do if the course turns out too slow, and why?
qa.a: Salma could practise the same skill with a small real dataset alongside it, because the target skills are what count and there is more than one way to learn them.

qa.q: How might Anjali see Salma's plan?
qa.a: Anjali may be pleased that the advice about SQL was taken and that Salma built the plan from evidence and not guesswork.

grounding: The person collects ten job listings, lists common skills, compares them with existing ones and plans courses to fill the gaps.

subtype: Approach: quit first and figure it out later [Pitfall]
passage:
Parveen was bored at the cooperative office in the kasba, tired of stamping forms she no longer read. One Monday she resigned. "I'll study full time and become a data analyst," she told her friend Jomon at his copy shop. Nobody had asked her how, and she had not asked herself either. She had no savings, no timetable and no course booked.

For three months she watched videos in the afternoon, opened a dozen tabs and finished none. She lay in bed mornings, telling herself she was on a break from thinking. The money in her account thinned to almost nothing.

In month four she took a job at a hardware store just to eat. The data plan was still a sentence in her notebook, only further away than before.

qa.q: Where did Parveen tell Jomon she would study full time?
qa.a: At his copy shop.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling in the months of drifting, and what shows it?
qa.a: Parveen felt stuck and increasingly anxious, shown by the untouched tabs, the late mornings and the dwindling money.

qa.q: What could Parveen have done before resigning, and why?
qa.a: Parveen could have saved some money and started a course while still working, because a plan and a safety net make the switch less risky.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Parveen's decision to resign?
qa.a: Jomon may have felt supportive but uneasy, having heard a big plan with no steps, and probably wanted to help more.

grounding: Bored at work, the person resigns to study full time with no plan or savings, then takes any job and the switch is delayed.

subtype: Approach: build a small project as a low-risk test [Action]
passage:
Saturday evening. Sahil stayed after the workshop at the community hall, laptop open, when Bidisha, a data analyst who ran the session, came to look. "You have a project?"

He nodded and turned the screen: a chart of local bus delays built from a public dataset, made over three weekends while he kept his job. She scrolled, asked what he meant by one column, and said, "Your method is sound. The chart hides the busiest hour. Fix that." A second professional, who was passing, added a comment about labels.

Sahil's stomach flipped as he listened, but he took notes. Riding the bus home, he thought: I didn't have to quit anything to find out if I like this. And I do.

qa.q: What did Sahil's chart show?
qa.a: Local bus delays.

qa.q: How was Sahil feeling as the two professionals commented on his work?
qa.a: Sahil felt nervous, with his stomach flipping, but also curious enough to keep taking notes.

qa.q: What could Sahil do next with the feedback, and why?
qa.a: Sahil could fix the hidden busy hour and show the improved version to the same two people, because it checks whether he can act on feedback.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see Sahil's project?
qa.a: Bidisha probably sees a keen beginner with a sound method, and saying the chart hides the busiest hour was a way of helping him improve.

grounding: While employed, the person completes a data project with public datasets and shows it to two professionals for feedback.

subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis over comparing many paths [Pitfall]
passage:
"Vidya, what is this?" asked her brother Hemant, holding up a printout from the sofa arm. It was a table with seven columns.

"My comparison. Data science, managing products, user-experience design, cloud. Salary, learning curve, demand, work-life balance..."

"How long have you been doing this?"

"Since April. I keep adding columns."

"It's September."

She folded her arms. "I want to choose properly. I can't just jump."

"Have you tried any of them? Even a free hour of a course?"

"No. I need more information first."

"More tables won't give it to you. Pick the top two and try each for two weeks."

Vidya stared at the table. "Five months," she said. "I've done five months of columns."

qa.q: How many columns did Vidya's table have?
qa.a: Seven columns.

qa.q: What is Vidya feeling when she says she cannot just jump?
qa.a: Vidya feels anxious about choosing wrongly, wanting certainty before committing, which is why she keeps adding columns.

qa.q: What could Vidya do next instead of adding another column, and why?
qa.a: Vidya could pick two paths and try a short course or task for each, because trying provides information that comparing on paper cannot.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Vidya's table?
qa.a: Hemant sees months of effort that have not moved her forward, and is trying to help her without hurting her feelings.

grounding: The person compares data science, product management, UX and cloud for months, making tables but never trying one.

subtype: Approach: bridge role with the same employer [Action]
passage:
The company had frozen new hiring, but Ujjwal did not want to wait for an opening. He asked Zubin, his manager, for ten minutes at the end of a crowded Thursday with two deadlines looming.

"I'd like to join the analytics project for the sales team," Ujjwal said. "I already do the monthly reports, so I know the data. I'd take the extra work on top of my own, just for a quarter."

Zubin sighed. "We're stretched, and I can't promise a formal move." He paused. "But Priya's group could use someone for the dashboards. I'll ask."

On Monday Ujjwal was pulled into the first meeting. It wasn't a new job, but it was one step closer to the field he wanted.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal already do for the company?
qa.a: The monthly reports.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel while asking Zubin, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt determined but somewhat nervous, since he chose a busy Thursday and offered to take on extra work to make the request easier to accept.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do if the analytics project turned out not to lead to a formal move, and why?
qa.a: Ujjwal could use the experience to build a portfolio and apply for openings elsewhere, because the skills gained still count toward the new field.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Ujjwal's request during a hiring freeze?
qa.a: Zubin is stretched and cannot promise a move, but may welcome a motivated team member who offers to help the analytics group.

grounding: The person asks the manager to join an analytics project in the current company, using transferable skills to move closer to the new field.

subtype: Approach: financial runway and pay-cut planning [Thinking]
passage:
I sat down with a calculator on Sunday, because worrying wasn't answering anything. I'm Sahil, and I wanted to know how long I could afford to change fields.

My savings cover about nine months of my current expenses. But the analytics jobs I'm looking at pay less at the start, so if I switch, the same savings cover fewer months. And I'd want two unpaid months for a course before applying. I wrote down what I'd accept: a starting salary no lower than a certain floor, and a limit of six months to land something, or I go back to a steady job.

Usha looked at my sheet and said, "You've found how fast you can go." It isn't a promise, but I can plan.

qa.q: How many months of expenses do Sahil's savings cover?
qa.a: About nine months.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel before doing the calculation?
qa.a: Sahil felt worried and stuck, since worrying without numbers was not answering anything.

qa.q: What could Sahil do if the calculation shows the plan is too tight, and why?
qa.a: Sahil could slow the switch by working while learning or saving more first, because the runway sets how fast the change can safely happen.

qa.q: How might Usha see Sahil's sheet?
qa.a: Usha probably finds it reassuring that Sahil has looked at the numbers honestly and set a limit, and the remark shows the plan is seen as sensible.

grounding: The person calculates how long savings last with a lower starting salary and unpaid learning, and sets an acceptable limit.
